So it's possible that a Weaken answer would attack this *Sampling* move, where the author reasons, "If it was true for *these* people, it must be true for people in general."
4	
5	But we can also attack the notion that the conclusion was even true for the people in the study. Were they examples of "humans who continued to hold onto acquired beliefs even in the absence of any credible evidence to support those beliefs"?
6	
7	If we want to fight that categorization, we either have to find a way to argue that the people in the study:
8	1. DIDN'T hold onto acquired beliefs, or
9	2. DID have credible evidence to support those beliefs (or both)
10	
11	We can't argue that first line of objection, because the evidence explicitly says that most of them persisted in their newly acquired beliefs.
12	
13	Okay, so is it possible that they *did* have credible evidence to support those beliefs? They probably didn't have credible evidence for those beliefs *prior* to the study, since we know it was reading the statements in the study that caused the people to form these new beliefs.
14	
15	But in between the time they're reading these statements and forming beliefs and the time, "Later," when they're told the statements were false, could they have gotten credible evidence to support the belief?
16	
17	Sure, I guess so. You could read a statement like, "Barack Obama plans to invest in a passenger spaceship to Mars" and then form the new belief, "Within the next 50 years, people will be able to take a passenger spaceship to Mars".
18	
19	Later, we tell you that Obama statement we provided you with was false, but when you got home that day, you Googled "passenger spaceship to Mars" and found out that Elon Musk was actually planning to do this. Your newly acquired belief has some credible evidence, in addition to the statement we provided.
20	
21	Thus, when we rescind the truth of those statements, it doesn't cause you to jettison that new belief you formed about "within 50 years, passenger travel to Mars". 4	
5	Those compromises give off the impression of ineffectuality, which people express dissatisfaction about.$lsat$),(2,$lsat$Evaluate$lsat$,$lsat$The conclusion is saying that reps are doing what they are elected to do, and it builds that case by defining what they're elected to do (compete for funds), telling us what's required of that (make compromises), and telling us a by-product of that requirement (you look ineffectual to some people).
6	
7	One of the most helpful observations we can make while reading this one is its *Conditional Conclusion*.
8	
9	We don't have to symbolize it, but if we did, it would look like this:
10

12	*dissatisfaction with - - - - - - - - -> what they were*
13	*their legislative reps elected to do*
14	
15	Fighting / Refuting / Rebutting / Contradicting a conditional means saying, "it's possible that the left side is true and the right side is false".
16	
17	So if we want to fight this conclusion, we need to argue that "it's possible that people are expressing dissatisfaction with their legislative reps, but the reps are **not** doing what they are elected to do".

20	
21	But what about other complaints? What people complain that "their representatives are making personally-enriching deals with foreign leaders"?
22	
23	Is that the representatives simply doing what they were elected to do?
24	
25	What if people complain that their representatives are making racist / sexist remarks? Is that the reps simply doing what they were elected to do?$lsat$),(3,$lsat$Goal$lsat$,$lsat$The correct answer will either lock us into the subject matter of the evidence, by giving some *Linking* idea like,

28

30

35	INSERT INTO lr_explanation_steps (explanation_id, position, label, body)
36	SELECT e.id, v.p, v.l, v.b FROM (SELECT e.id FROM lr_explanations e JOIN lr_questions q ON q.id=e.question_id WHERE q.preptest=113 AND q.section=4 AND q.question_number=13 AND e.style IN ('single','standard') AND EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM lr_explanation_choice_notes n WHERE n.explanation_id=e.id) AND NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM lr_explanation_steps s WHERE s.explanation_id=e.id) ORDER BY (e.style='single') DESC LIMIT 1) e, (VALUES (0,$lsat$Conclusion$lsat$,$lsat$The one-sided facial rash was caused by prolonged contact with telephones.$lsat$),(1,$lsat$Evidence$lsat$,$lsat$Several patients had a rash on just one side of their faces, and in each case the rash was on the same side as the patient's telephone use.$lsat$),(2,$lsat$Evaluate$lsat$,$lsat$When we're dealing with a "diagnosis / hypothesis / explanation", we know we're dealing with *Explain Curious Fact*.

77	
78	This is an often used LSAT trope. More people die using the crosswalk because way more people cross there than jaywalking.
79	
80	It's kinda like saying, "Flying in a plane is safer than jumping out of a place, but more people die flying in a plane". That's because millions of people fly every year, but only thousands jump out of a plane.
81	
82	Or like saying, "Covid is a much milder illness than Ebola. Yet, more people die of covid than die of Ebola." That's because tens of millions of people get covid and only a few thousand get Ebola.
83

87	
88	GOAL

86	
87	*Inspected ------------------------> Safe*$lsat$),(1,$lsat$Evidence$lsat$,$lsat$*Inspected ---> ~Infected*$lsat$),(2,$lsat$Evaluate$lsat$,$lsat$The "therefore" shows us the claim we're trying to prove. On Sufficient Assumption, there are two big questions we can ask about the Conclusion:
88	
89	1. Is there any New Term (that isn't ever discussed in the evidence)?
90	
91	2. Can I / should I write this conclusion as a "long conditional"?
92	
93	When it comes to #1, yes, there was a New Term in the conclusion that was never discussed or defined in the evidence: *safe to eat*.
94	
95	So it's a guarantee that the correct answer will have to say "safe to eat" or something equivalent. After all, the correct answer combines with the evidence and allows us to derive the conclusion.
96	
97	If you had all these claims,
98	a = b
99	b = c
100	c = d
101	you could never derive the claim
102	a = x
103	because we don't have any givens about "x".
104	
105	When it comes to #2, we're motivated to write the conclusion as a long-conditional so that we can better see the missing piece we need.
106	
107	The conclusion is one big logic path we're trying to build.
108	*Inspected ----------------------------------> Safe*
109	
110	The evidence and the answer we pick are the building blocks for that logic path. The one premise we have is this:
111	*No fruit that was inspected is infected*.
112	
113	The other statement, "if infected, then rotten" is irrelevant to our conclusion. Our conclusion is about **inspected** fruit, and none of the inspected fruit is infected. So that first sentence is what you might call a "Fake Premise". It looks like it could be relevant, but it has nothing to do with our conclusion.
114	
115	So how do we turn our one premise (the 2nd sentence) into a conditional?
116	
117	**No A's are B = All A's are ~B = A → ~B**
118	No inspected are infected = All inspected are not infected
119	*Inspected → ~Infected*
120	
121	We're trying to prove this,
122	
123	*Inspected ----------------------------------> Safe*
124	
125	and this is what we have so far
126	
127	*Inspected ----> ~Infected*
128	
129	So what are we missing?
130	*~Infected ---------------> Safe*
131	
132	If you want to do this problem more conversationally, then just work backwards from the conclusion. You're trying to prove that "anything inspected is safe".
133	
134	What were we told about stuff that was inspected?
135	We were told that it **isn't infected**.
136	
137	What were we told about stuff that **isn't infected**?
138	Nothing.
139	
140	So we know that a possible answer could be
141	"if **isn't infected**, then **safe to eat**"$lsat$),(3,$lsat$Goal$lsat$,$lsat$We're looking for
142	
143	"if **isn't infected**, then **safe to eat**"
144	
145	but since we know that Sufficient Assumption loves to hide the correct answer via contrapositive, we should also look for
146	"if it's **isn't safe** to eat, then it is **infected**"$lsat$)) v(p,l,b)

160	SELECT e.id, v.p, v.l, v.b FROM (SELECT e.id FROM lr_explanations e JOIN lr_questions q ON q.id=e.question_id WHERE q.preptest=124 AND q.section=2 AND q.question_number=20 AND e.style IN ('single','standard') AND EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM lr_explanation_choice_notes n WHERE n.explanation_id=e.id) AND NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM lr_explanation_steps s WHERE s.explanation_id=e.id) ORDER BY (e.style='single') DESC LIMIT 1) e, (VALUES (0,$lsat$Conclusion (Therefore)$lsat$,$lsat$There are some days in Hillview when the wind blows from the east and the smog reaches unsafe levels.$lsat$),(1,$lsat$Evidence$lsat$,$lsat$On some hot days in Hillview, the wind blows from the east.
161	On some hot days in Hillview, the smog reaches unsafe levels.$lsat$),(2,$lsat$Evaluate$lsat$,$lsat$Because both premises and the conclusion are quantified *Some* claims, we might want to think about *Trait Overlap* inferences:
162	
163	Some A's are B Most A's are B
164	All A's are C Most A's are C

167	There aren't any trait overlap inferences where you combine two Some facts about the same group.

172

31	-- PT127-S1-Q19 (Notes-only)
32	INSERT INTO lr_explanation_steps (explanation_id, position, label, body)
33	SELECT e.id, v.p, v.l, v.b FROM (SELECT e.id FROM lr_explanations e JOIN lr_questions q ON q.id=e.question_id WHERE q.preptest=127 AND q.section=1 AND q.question_number=19 AND e.style IN ('single','standard') AND EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM lr_explanation_choice_notes n WHERE n.explanation_id=e.id) AND NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM lr_explanation_steps s WHERE s.explanation_id=e.id) ORDER BY (e.style='single') DESC LIMIT 1) e, (VALUES (0,$lsat$Conclusion (therefore)$lsat$,$lsat$We have no obligation not to cut down trees.$lsat$),(1,$lsat$Evidence$lsat$,$lsat$There can be no obligation to an entity unless that entity has a corresponding right.
34	
35	(If an entity doesn't have a right, then there's no obligation to that entity)
36	
37	Trees don't have rights.$lsat$),(2,$lsat$Evaluate$lsat$,$lsat$This argument is famously hard to read. The author provides a conditional relationship in the 2nd sentence:
38	
39	*Entity has no rights → No obligation to entity*
40	
41	Then the author draws an Intermediate Conclusion with "So" that is just spelling out how conditional logic works. In our case, it's spelling out how the contrapositive of what we just wrote would sound, if it were applied to trees:
42	
43	*Do have obligation to trees → trees have rights*
44	
45	We're not going to spend any mental energy fighting that conclusion, since it is airtight. If I introduce a rule that says "You can't be X unless you're Y", then it's absolutely valid for me to then conclude, "So if Pam is X, then Pam is Y".
46	
47	When the author tells us "But trees don't have rights", she is triggering the contrapositive of that Intermediate Conclusion.
48	
49	So, implicitly, she is allowing us to infer, "Okay, if trees don't have rights, **then we have no obligation toward trees**."
50	
51	How is that different from the actual Conclusion?
52	
53	*we have no obligation toward trees*
54	*vs.*
55	*we have no obligation not to cut down trees*
56	
57	There's a good chance we'd be confused enough by the stimulus that we'd have to go check out answer with only a foggy sense of what's going on.
58	
59	But if we're lucky, we see that tiny gap looks like this:
60	
61	"If we don't have an obligation toward trees, then we don't have an obligation not to cut down trees." This gap is acting like the only obligation we needed to worry about was one toward trees. If we we're not obliged toward trees, then we're in the clear --- no obligation at all.
62	
63	If we were trying to argue the Anti-Conclusion, we'd be thinking, "GIVEN THAT we have no obligation towards trees, HOW COULD WE STILL ARGUE THAT we **do** have some obligation not to cut down trees?"
64	
65	What came to my mind was
66	1. I'm obliged not to cut down the tree in my neighbor's yard, not because I have an obligation towards that tree, but because I'm obliged to respect my neighbor's property.
67	
68	2. I'm obliged not to cut down the trees in the Amazon Rain Forest, not because I have an obligation towards those trees, but because I have an obligation not to exacerbate climate change for future generations of humans.$lsat$),(3,$lsat$Goal$lsat$,$lsat$Look for an answer addressing the gap of, "If we don't have an obligation toward trees, then we don't have an obligation, period." Or look for an answer ruling out some other way in which we'd be obliged not to cut down trees.$lsat$)) v(p,l,b)
69	ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING;

72	INSERT INTO lr_explanation_steps (explanation_id, position, label, body)
73	SELECT e.id, v.p, v.l, v.b FROM (SELECT e.id FROM lr_explanations e JOIN lr_questions q ON q.id=e.question_id WHERE q.preptest=127 AND q.section=1 AND q.question_number=25 AND e.style IN ('single','standard') AND EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM lr_explanation_choice_notes n WHERE n.explanation_id=e.id) AND NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM lr_explanation_steps s WHERE s.explanation_id=e.id) ORDER BY (e.style='single') DESC LIMIT 1) e, (VALUES (0,$lsat$Statements$lsat$,$lsat$*conditional (it is A to be B:* B → A)
74	
75	It's hard to grow cacti in a humid climate.
76	*Humid climate → hard to grow cacti*
77	
78	It's hard to raise orange trees in a cold climate.
79	*Cold climate → hard to raise orange tree*
80	
81	In most parts of the country, it's easy to grow cacti or easy to raise orange trees.$lsat$),(1,$lsat$Evaluate$lsat$,$lsat$The correct answer on Must Be False almost always does one of two things:
82	1. Contradicts a conditional relationship provided
83	2. Contradicts an available inference we can make by combining claims.
84	
85	There are two quasi-conditionals in the first two sentences. So a correct answer could say something like, "Most people who live in humid climates grow cacti very easily", or "in most parts of Arrendale, which has a permanently cold climate thanks to Queen Elsa, it's easy to raise orange trees".
86	
87	Can we combine claims to infer anything?
88	
89	We see the *Overlapping Concept* of "easy/difficult to grow cacti" and "easy/difficult to raise orange trees". This suggests that we can combine these claims.
90	
91	The contrapositive to our conditionals would be,
92	
93	*not difficult → not humid*
94	*to grow cacti*
95	
96	*not difficult to → not cold*
97	*raise orange trees*
98	
99	If they tell us that in most parts of the country it's easy to grow cacti or easy to raise orange trees, then we know that in most parts of the country it's either "not humid", "not cold", or both.$lsat$),(2,$lsat$Goal$lsat$,$lsat$Look for an answer that contradicts either of the two conditionals in the first two sentences,
100	
101	or look for an answer that contradicts the inference we made by applying the final sentence to those two conditionals, to derive:
102	
103	*most parts of country → ~Humid or ~Cold*$lsat$)) v(p,l,b)
104	ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING;

106	-- PT127-S1-Q26 (Notes-only)
107	INSERT INTO lr_explanation_steps (explanation_id, position, label, body)
108	SELECT e.id, v.p, v.l, v.b FROM (SELECT e.id FROM lr_explanations e JOIN lr_questions q ON q.id=e.question_id WHERE q.preptest=127 AND q.section=1 AND q.question_number=26 AND e.style IN ('single','standard') AND EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM lr_explanation_choice_notes n WHERE n.explanation_id=e.id) AND NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM lr_explanation_steps s WHERE s.explanation_id=e.id) ORDER BY (e.style='single') DESC LIMIT 1) e, (VALUES (0,$lsat$Statements$lsat$,$lsat$*conditionals* (always, nothing but)
109	
110	Common → Always progressing
111	sense
112	
113	Common → collection of time-tested
114	sense theories found useful
115	
116	*conditional* (when)
117	
118	Alternate theory eventually
119	more useful than → supplant theories
120	common sense in common sense
121	
122	*causal* (causes, because)
123	
124	The process of newer, common
125	more useful theories ⇢ sense
126	eventually supplanting progresses
127	theories in common sense
128	
129	Common sense absorbs Common sense
130	new theories slowly ⇢ always has some
131	obsolete stuff$lsat$),(1,$lsat$Evaluate$lsat$,$lsat$We're very attracted to Conditional or Causal indicator wording, when we're doing Must Be True and Most Supported. And that's because often conditional as well as causal statements **chain** together. If A leads to B, and B leads to C, they can test us on our understanding that A leads to C.
132	
133	But then other times we get a random mess of stuff, like this problem. Diagramming these statements is probably not going to help us, since they don't really chain together. And since there are a few conditional ideas and a couple causal ones, should we anticipate a conditional chain or a causal chain?
134	
135	In short, we don't know. However, the final sentence does have a **pivot** (but / yet / however). Usually, when an Inference paragraph *Ends with a Pivot*, the correct answer deals with the tension created by that pivot idea.
136	
137	What does it tell us, if anything, that because common sense absorbs new theories slowly, it always contains some obsolete theories?
138	
139	"Obsolete" means that something is no longer widely used or believed, or its functionality has been superseded. The iPod and iPhones made listening to music on CD's obsolete.
140	
141	So if some theories in common sense are obsolete, it's because alternative theories have already proven themselves more useful. I guess common sense is like a big corporation. Even when smaller businesses innovate better ways, the big corporation's pace of change is glacial, so it has some outmoded ways of doing things.$lsat$),(2,$lsat$Goal$lsat$,$lsat$Let's look for anything provable, possibly dealing with the tension created by the fact that common sense always contains some obsolete ideas.
142	
143	We know three things about "common sense"
144	- always progressing
145	- a collection of theories that have been tested over time and found useful
146	- always contains some obsolete theories
147	
148	Maybe the correct answer will speak to an overlap between some of those traits.$lsat$)) v(p,l,b)
149	ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING;

It's the fragmentation of the forest that imperils songbirds, **because** that introduces open spaces and corridors in forests, which reduces the distance from songbird nests to unforested areas, which reduces the songbirds' protection from predators.$lsat$),(2,$lsat$Evaluate$lsat$,$lsat$Whenever we read Main Conclusion or Role paragraphs, we look out for Conclusions appearing **earlier** than the supporting ideas.
